e.etymology: A variant of Elsworth, an English surname from a Cambridgeshire village whose Old English name means the enclosure of a man called Elli.
A variant of Carlene, a 20th-century coinage from Carl and the -ene ending of Marlene and Charlene. Carl, like Charles, comes from a Germanic word for a free man.
A short form of Theodosia and Theodora, Greek names built on theos, god, and words for giving. The silent film star Theda Bara, born Theodosia Goodman, brought it into fashion in the 1910s.
namesakes: Theda Bara (silent film star known as The Vamp)

e.etymology: A spelling of Nancy, which began in medieval England as a pet form of Ann and Agnes. Ann comes from Hebrew Hannah, grace or favor.
A variant of Kristin and Kristen, Scandinavian forms of Christina, and for boys of Kristian. All go back to Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
The word name Dawn with a feminine -a added, a 20th-century formation. In much of the US it sounds the same as Donna.
A respelling of Shirley, an English place name and surname from Old English scir (bright, or shire) and leah (clearing). Shirley became a girls' name in the 1800s.
In the US a short form of Jeremiah, usually said like Jerry. In Finland Jere, said YEH-reh, is a short form of Jeremias, the same biblical name.
A spelling of Doc, the nickname short for doctor, registered as a given name in the American South in the 1800s. Dock is also a surname.
namesakes: Dock Ellis (Pirates pitcher who threw a 1970 no-hitter)

e.etymology: A variant of Noreen, the English form of Irish Noirin, little Nora. In Ireland Nora began as a short form of Honora, from Latin honor.
A variant of Janet and Janette, diminutives of Jane. Jane is a feminine form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A variant of Curtis, an Anglo-Norman surname and given name from Old French curteis, courteous or well-bred.
A respelling of Elizabeth, from the Greek form of Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. In the Bible Elizabeth is the mother of John the Baptist.
A respelling of Melissa, from Greek melissa, honeybee.
An American girls' name of the 1970s, close in sound to Charisse and Cherie and to French cerise, cherry.
An American compound of Carol and Lee. Carol began as a short form of Caroline, a feminine form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man.
A spelling of Debra, the 20th-century short spelling of Deborah, from Hebrew devorah, bee. Deborah is the prophetess and judge of the Book of Judges.
A respelling of Michelle, the French feminine of Michel (Michael), from Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God?.
An English surname from Old English hlynn (roaring stream, waterfall) and wudu (wood, forest). Linwood is the sister spelling.
The Latinized form of Adolph, from Old High German adal (noble) and wolf. The Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus made the Latin form familiar.
e.note: One step from Adolf, a name most people still link with Hitler.

e.etymology: A spelling of Christine, the French form of Christina, from Latin Christiana, a Christian woman.
An American name of the 1970s and 1980s that joins the Sher- of Sherry and Cheryl to the -ita ending of Juanita and Anita.
An English surname from the medieval name Ailmer, Old English Aethelmaer, noble and famous. A second source is the Gloucestershire village of Elmore, named for a bank where elms grew.
An English surname from a variant of Hubert, a Germanic name joining hug (mind, heart) and beraht (bright). Its 1896 peak came as Garret Hobart was elected vice president.
A Yiddish women's name, generally taken as a form of Jette, the German short form of Henriette, and sometimes linked with Judith. It was common among Jewish immigrant families around 1900.
namesakes: Grandma Yetta (Fran's grandmother on The Nanny)

e.etymology: A respelling of Kelly, from the Irish surname O Ceallaigh, descendant of Ceallach, an old personal name of debated meaning, often given as bright-headed or as strife.
A 20th-century spelling of Cindy, the pet form of Cynthia. Cynthia was a title of the goddess Artemis, born on Mount Kynthos on the island of Delos.
namesakes: Cyndi Lauper (pop singer, Girls Just Want to Have Fun)

assoc.t: Cyndi Lauper, singer of Girls Just Want to Have Fun

e.etymology: A spelling of Jackie, the pet form of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques. Jacques is the French form of James and Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov, traditionally supplanter.
A turn-of-the-century American name in the family of Lora and Lorie, pet forms of Laura.
A spelling of Sharon, the Hebrew name of the fertile coastal plain of Israel. Sherron was mostly a girls' name at its 1940s peak; recent American use is for boys, often with the stress on the end.
An English surname from Old French brunel, a diminutive of brun, brown, first a nickname for someone with brown hair or a dark complexion.
